author: Ross Reily
title: Jackson has uphill battle for economic development, demographer says - NewsBreak
text:
By Ross Reily ,
12 hours ago In the 2021 census, Jackson's population dropped below 150,000 for the first time since before 1970.
The shrinking continued with the release of data from the 2022 census estimates, which revealed a 2.5% drop for the state's capital city.
Jackson's population stood at 145,995. The drop of 3,766 from 2021 to 2022 made it the fastest-shrinking city with at least 50,000 residents in the United States.
Three years later, the estimates are that Jackson's population has dropped even further to fewer than 136,000.
Bradley Schurman , a demographer and author who has spent his career decoding what is reshaping economies and American cities, said Jackson has a hill to climb to achieve economic development goals.
Schurman visited Jackson recently as part of the due diligence of writing his upcoming book, "The Geography of Prosperity: A new map of the American Dream." After a visit to Jackson a few weeks ago, Schurman had some thoughts about what is going on in the state's largest city.
In preparation for writing his book, Schurman made a commitment that if he were going to write about a city, he would visit it and try to talk with city leaders. So, he came to Jackson in April. However, no one from the City of Jackson made themselves available to visit with him while he was in town.
"I have to tell you, Downtown Jackson is pretty jarring," Schurman told the Clarion Ledger. "I took the train in from Memphis, walked through downtown. Everyone who I met there was kind, courteous, generous. But the first thing I noticed was desolation. I feel like during my time there, I saw maybe 10 people on the streets. That says a lot about a place. The people that I did see were a couple of police officers, some government workers and a TV reporter standing in front of the (federal) courthouse."
Where does Jackson rank? Schurman also developed a place-based framework to evaluate long-term civic viability, known as The Geography of Prosperity Index .
On that index, Jackson ranked 198 out of 250 cities in America.
Jackson has an overall score of 45.3 out of 100. According to the rankings, the drag on Jackson comes primarily from "Governance & Foresight," which scored a 19.5 out of 100 (231st of 250) putting the city below the national average and pulling the composite score down.
"As a Southeast metro with rapid population growth, persistent equity gaps and governance capacity still catching up to city scale, Jackson sits in below-average territory, a position that reflects structural challenges rather than a single bad data point — reversing it will require sustained investment in governance capacity (that) builds fast enough to match economic growth and equity gaps narrow rather than widen," according to the comments on The Prosperity Index.
While Schurman's Prosperity Index points out challenges for Jackson, Schurman said he wants to see the city succeed as well as every American city.
"When city leaders are not willing to talk, that says loads. It says more about the problem," Schurman said. "So, I talked to the locals while I was there."
What Schurman found was that Jacksonians want to move forward and for the city to be better.
"There is such a depth of civic pride, amongst the people that I met," Schurman said. "They were positive despite some of the clearly visible challenges. That alone shows a certain degree of resilience."
While Schurman was not able to track down someone from the City of Jackson ahead of his visit, he said he did not reach out to others who might have given him a little more perspective of Jackson and the area, such as Downtown Jackson Partners, Greater Jackson Chamber Partnership, the Hinds County Economic Development Authority or Mississippi Development Authority. He did not even reach out to local media for his visit, organizations that might have offered more insight into Jackson.
What are the positives in Downtown Jackson? Schurman was not aware of developments such as the emergence of Kumar Bhavanasi on the Downtown Jackson scene.
Bhavanasi, a New Jersey developer who owns 35 shopping developments throughout the nation, has purchased more than 1 million square feet of property in Downtown Jackson, which includes 192,000 square feet in the Pinnacle Building, another 30,000 at the Deposit Guaranty Building as well as the 1,735-space parking garage with first-floor commercial space connected to the Pinnacle building. Bhavanasi also owns Regions Plaza, the tallest building in Mississippi, which has 346,159 square feet and is located within the Capitol Complex Improvement District. Most recently, Bhavanasi purchased the former Marriott building and the Electric Building at 308 E. Pearl Street.
"I am not aware of the developments (with Bhavanasi)," Schurman said. "That can be a problem too as not having diversity in ownership in an area can lead to problems. But I will say that in this instance, it does seem positive that someone is investing in the downtown area."
While in Jackson, Schurman ate dinner at The Mayflower Cafe , which he said was the highlight of his trip. While he was there someone suggested the gumbo as well as onion rings.
"The young lady told me it would be a crime if I didn't have the onion rings," Schurman said. "She was right. They were the best I have ever had. So, I had this really positive experience in this place, but, as I am looking out over this street, I felt like I was in that Edward Hopper painting "The Nighthawks" with that neon glow on my face, but outside is nothingness."
Suggestions for Downtown Jackson While he has his takes on Downtown Jackson, Schurman said he would like to see the city take some action similar to what South Bend, Indiana, has done over the past decade.
"One big note for context is that Jackson’s score isn’t a condemnation or a death sentence," Schurman said. "It’s a diagnostic. And my book, which comes out next year, highlights solutions from places that were written off years ago that have clawed their way back. Many of these cities are in the Midwest, including South Bend, which have seen population gains in recent years."
Key initiatives in South Bend have included a $785 million downtown boom, the SMART Streets initiative, and the redevelopment of former industrial sites such as Ignition Park. Recent efforts focus on building over 500 new housing units, boosting streetscape and enhancing the riverfront to create a walkable, mixed-use environment.
What's next for Jackson? While Schurman said that not every city can be treated the same, he does see similarities in Jackson and South Bend.
"Jackson is not a lost cause," Schurman said. "There are things that can be done, like traffic patterns, small things and big things. But there are options. The one thing I would say is to face the problems head on."
Ross Reily is a writer for the Clarion Ledger, part of the USA TODAY Network. He can be reached at rreily@gannett.com or 601-573-2952. You can follow him on the X platform, formerly known as Twitter @GreenOkra1.
